title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
hookLine: a prison at midnight, a river that gives way, and God come down as a baby
carry: avatara: god comes down in the darkest hour
tomorrow: why do families bring Ganesha home, then give him to the water?
last: WHERE RAMA'S STORY IS TOLD, HANUMAN IS THERE.

cards: It's nearly midnight, and in temples across India, and in living rooms in Houston and Leicester and Singapore, people who have fasted all day are waiting. There's a small cradle decorated with flowers.
At twelve, the conch shells blow, the bells ring, and somebody sets a tiny image of a baby into the cradle and starts rocking it. A birthday, kept at the exact hour. Why midnight?
The answer starts in a prison cell.

teach.b: Janma means birth. Ashtami means the eighth: the eighth day of the waning moon. The story is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana.

In Mathura, the tyrant Kamsa is driving his cousin Devaki and her new husband Vasudeva after their wedding, when a voice from the sky tells him: the eighth child of this woman will kill you. Kamsa locks them in prison.

teach.h: THE EIGHTH CHILD, BORN IN A PRISON.
teach.b: Child after child is born there, and Kamsa kills them; the seventh, the text says, is carried away to another womb. Then comes the eighth.
He is born at midnight, and the Bhagavata says the whole world grows calm and bright at that hour. The baby first appears to his parents in a divine form, then becomes an ordinary newborn.

teach.h: THE CHAINS FALL. THE RIVER GIVES WAY.
teach.b: Vasudeva's chains fall away. The guards sleep. The doors open by themselves.
Vasudeva lifts the baby and walks out into a storm. The great serpent Shesha spreads its hoods over them. At the Yamuna, swollen with rain, the river gives way.
In Gokul, the cowherd Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth. Vasudeva leaves his son there and carries her baby back.

This is the heart of a big Hindu teaching: avatara, God coming down. In the Bhagavad Gita, the grown Krishna says it himself: whenever dharma declines and wrong rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good.
So people don't stay up only for a birthday.
They stay up for that promise, kept in the darkest hour, in the most locked-up place.

how: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast through the day, sing devotional songs in the evening, and at midnight celebrate Krishna's birth with conch shells, bells and a decorated cradle, then break the fast.

o: the full-moon night for honoring one's teacher
a family rite for naming a newborn baby
Krishna's birthday, kept at midnight on the eighth

s: the Bhagavata places the birth at midnight, which is why many keep the festival until twelve.
Vasudeva has to break the chains himself
the chains fall away, the guards sleep, and the doors open on their own.
in the Gita, Krishna says he comes age after age when dharma declines
that's avatara, God coming down, and it's why a midnight birth in a prison matters.

games.q: a little cousin asks why God would be born in a prison instead of a palace. what fits today's teaching?
o: Hindus teach that God comes down where dharma is darkest: avatara. the prison is the point.
it was a mistake in the story.
Krishna wanted to test his parents first.
games.why: in the Gita Krishna promises to come whenever wrong rises. his birth in Kamsa's prison, at midnight, is that promise kept.

practice: Dim the lights or close your eyes, and sit in the dark without hurrying it. If you pray, softly say Krishna's name, or the line many sing at midnight: Nand ke anand bhayo, jai Kanhaiya Lal ki, joy in Nanda's house.
If you don't, simply wait for something good, the way people wait for twelve.

wordCard.voice: Janmashtami. The birthday on the eighth: Krishna born at midnight in Kamsa's prison, God come down, kept by many Hindus with a fast and a cradle.

orig.note: Sanskrit janma (birth) + aṣṭamī (the eighth lunar day): Krishna's birthday.
